claims.claim: Epiphanius was bishop of Constantia (Salamis), the metropolis of the island of Cyprus.
Epiphanius was born after 310 and died in 403.
Epiphanius was nominated as bishop in 367 and fulfilled the duties of the episcopate for nearly forty years.
The collection of homilies traditionally ascribed to a 'Saint Epiphanius, bishop' are dated in the late fifth or sixth century and are not connected with Epiphanius of Salamis by modern scholars.
The homily In divini corporis sepulturum (CPG 3768; BHG 808e), attributed to Epiphanius of Salamis, was intended for liturgical reading on Holy Saturday.
There is no argument for a genuinely Epiphanian authorship of the sermon In divini corporis sepulturum.
The Greek text of the homily attributed to Epiphanius is available in Migne's Patrologia Graeca vol. 43, coll. 439-464 (= Homilia II in Sabbato magno).
The homily attributed to Epiphanius survives in numerous versions in ancient languages including Syriac, Armenian, Georgian, Arabic, and Old Slavonic.
The homily attributed to Epiphanius was popular among the Copts, as indicated by numerous Egyptian Arabic manuscripts.
The homily is divided in two parts: the first is a praise to Joseph of Arimathea, and the second part recounts the harrowing of hell and contains a discourse of Jesus to Adam.
The homily is counted among the most curious Patristic works concerning the harrowing of hell.
